title: I made my first deck builder, thanks to AI.
author: iamhadal
selftext:
I did multiple tech projects over the last 20 years, mostly around web development and platforms. I never really created games, although that's something I always wanted to do.

For the last couple of years, I started to experiment with AI to create games. After a few projects purely on JavaScript and HTML, I finally made a "true" game using Godot. I am releasing the first beta version today.

About the process: 99% of the code and the art was generated via AI. I took advantage of my ChatGPT Plus subscription and developed the code with Codex, using Godot as a game engine.

I created all the art assets directly with ChatGPT using standard prompts to try to keep a consistent style.

The game design part was the result of many iterations using ChatGPT to bounce ideas and refine them. AI wasn't really here to create ideas, but it was helpful in being a sparring partner to discuss ideas and refine them over time.

Things I learned in the process:

* Codex does a good job as you break down the task into smaller chunks.
* From time to time, it is useful to ask Codex to just review some specific systems, propose ameliorations, and implement the ones that make sense. It avoids accumulating technical debt over time.
* Heavy testing is key to detect bugs and flaws in the implementation.
* Human validation and Agmen is a bottleneck. I don't really use multiple agents at the same time, as ultimately it will only slow me down when I have to review everything.I prefer a more modular approach where I create a feature or content, test it, validate it, and move on.
* ChatGPT Image 2 is a solid model, but using it only with ChatGPT makes it complicated to manage drift. For the future, I would consider tools like Scenario to better ensure consistency.
* If I am to release a commercial version, I will switch to human-made art to make it more unique and relatable, although AI might still be used in the process.
* The main difficulty came from overly ambitious prompts and compiling and exporting in WebGL, for example.
* Godot is very friendly for AI development, as you can also develop the interface from prompts since everything is stored as text. It might be possible in Unity as well, but I didn't deep dive much as Godot is a free alternative.

If you want to help the game, you can check it out on [itch.io](http://itch.io); the link is below. Any feedback is appreciated.

It is an early playtest version, the first one available, so expect some potential balance issues and bugs, of course.

[Agmen on itch.io](https://hadalgames.itch.io/agmen)

comments.author: PairOfPixelsGS
comments.body: Hey, congrats! How accurate was ChatGPT on implementing the features, especially the more complex ones? Did you have to fix a lot of things? Nice work

replies.author: iamhadal
replies.body:
I've used Codex, not ChatGPT, although it does use the same underlying models.

I was quite surprised how good it was. In 75% of the cases, everything worked directly. It does not mean that the code was perfect, but it did work.  When it failed, it was sometimes because the scope I gave was too large.

What I did in addition was to regularly ask Codex to review specific systems (e.g. if I saw bugs starting to appear). It identified systems that could be improved and proposed several solutions. That allowed them to keep the same codebase all the time.

replies.author: iamhadal
replies.body:
Yes, it can be a bit frustrating. To be honest, in my case, Codex did a good job on the first attempt with quite detailed instructions.

One thing I need for this or other systems is to ask Codex to expose different parameters in an external JSON file. That way, I could just tweak the value sensitivity in the JSON and try those tweaks very quickly.
